<reason>Both sides built plausible cases on-mechanism, but B consistently won the decisive exchanges. B's falsifiability pressure (B3.1) forced A to construct a test (A4.1) that B then credibly characterized as absorbing Japan's real-world childcare expansion; A's "fund capacity" answer to the waiting-list leakage rejoinder implicitly conceded B's timing critique. B's pull-forward-timing rebuttal (B4.1-4.2, sharpened in B5.2) went essentially unanswered on the biology of the first-to-second-child gap, leaving a live route to victory. A's strongest card — that B's "recurring bonus" pivot abandons the motion's "one-off" framing — was real and landed in A4.4/A5.4, but B retained a motion-compliant core via the timing argument, so the drift cost B only partially. B's rebuttals were sharper, better sequenced, and better crystallized; A's case was coherent but repeatedly needed escape hatches (tiny units, half-measures, fund capacity later) that B named and punished. Marginal deduction for B's clipped opening.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B2's "rigged scoreboard / escape hatch" rebuttal was the turning point: it named A's pattern of reclassifying every housing or childcare failure as not-really-trying, then showed A's "real" policy (public rental, fee caps, provider subsidies) relocated rather than fixed the leakage problem into queues and provider costs. B4.5-4.6 extended it into the "collapse into transfers" and unfalsifiability attacks that A never fully escaped.</best_rebuttal>
